blockMcqs.question: At its core, what does an LLM actually do?
options: Looks facts up in a database
Plans a whole paragraph in advance
Searches the live internet per query
blockMcqs.explanation: Generation is repeated next-token prediction; weights store patterns, not a fact store.

blockMcqs.question: Roughly how many words is 1,000 tokens?
blockMcqs.explanation: One token is about 0.75 words, so 1,000 tokens is roughly 750.

blockMcqs.question: Why does attention make a 100K-token prompt expensive?
options: It stores every token on disk
Cost grows with the square of length
It re-tokenizes the prompt each step
Longer prompts need a bigger model
blockMcqs.explanation: Every token attends to every other, so compute scales as O(n²).

blockMcqs.question: How does a chat app give an LLM "memory" across turns?
options: The model stores state between calls
Prior turns are re-sent every request
blockMcqs.explanation: Each call is stateless, so history is resent — which is why long chats cost more.

blockMcqs.question: How does RAG reduce hallucination?
options: It lowers the temperature to zero
It hands the model real text to answer from
blockMcqs.explanation: Grounding turns the model into a reader of supplied facts, not a recaller.

blockMcqs.question: What lets an agent decide to invoke a tool?
blockMcqs.explanation: The model returns structured arguments; your code runs the tool and feeds results back.

blockMcqs.question: When is fine-tuning the right choice over RAG?
options: To enforce a consistent output format
blockMcqs.explanation: Fine-tuning shapes behavior and style; facts belong in retrieval.

blockMcqs.question: Why is pasting an entire corpus into a huge window risky?
options: It can bury the relevant fact
blockMcqs.explanation: "Lost in the middle": long prompts cost more and hide the key passage.
